identified_problem: Oral assessments are rated Weak on workload: 10-minute interviews for 100 students are estimated at about 1,000 minutes of staff time, and live checkoffs overran planned times and took about 80% of TA office-hour time [R84], [R95]. They are only Moderate on scalability and feasibility for the same reason [S011], [S012]. They are also Moderate on authorship, process visibility and appropriate AI use, because an oral shows reasoning on demand but not the working process or how AI was used unless it is paired with logs or repositories [R79], [R81], and on equity, because viva performance may reflect anxiety or language proficiency [R81], [R51].
recommended_redesign: Use short, structured vivas of about 10 minutes, with scripted core questions, a rubric and booked appointments with time limits [R80], [R95].
Anchor questions in the student's own artefact, commit history or prompt log, include live modification requests, and ask how AI output was checked [R80], [R81], [R79], [J4].
For large cohorts, use sampled or risk-based orals (for example a random 20% sample) or secure orals only at key programme points such as capstones, instead of universal vivas [S009], [R68], [R04].
Provide second attempts, quieter rooms and other accommodations, and triangulate the oral with other evidence rather than treating it as decisive [R95], [R81].
justification: Finding: in a computing module, take-home scores averaged about 83.8% but viva scores about 35.2%, and many high scorers could not explain their own code [R81]; 10-minute vivas with live modification requests ran for over 750 students and gave clearly different marks to members of the same group [R80]. Finding: the staff cost is high, at about 1,000 minutes per 100 students [R84] and about 80% of TA office-hour time for 237 students [R95]. Interpretation: orals are among the best-evidenced ways to verify individual understanding, so the redesign keeps them but limits their length and coverage and ties them to process evidence, so that the cost is proportionate to the stakes [R68], [R81].
implementation_considerations: Cohort: full individual vivas are workable for small cohorts of up to about 30 [R94], [R79]; for medium cohorts a viva plus live demo ran within normal delivery for 60 students [R81]; for large cohorts orals were feasible only with short formats, many staff, TA schedules, sampling or rotating tutor conversations [R80], [R95], [S009], [J4].

Staff time: budget about 1,000 staff minutes per 100 students for 10-minute interviews [R84]; the 750-student implementation reported no staff-time data [R80], and current viva practice used at least two evaluators per session [S156].

Consistency: human examiners varied much more than LLM graders (CoV 32.69% against 8.44%), so rubrics and moderation are needed; automated text-based vivas were tested with over 250 students but not for integrity outcomes [S156].
Equity: guidelines warn that heavy use of oral formats may disadvantage non-native speakers and students with disabilities, and no study measured outcomes by group [R51], [R81], [R11].
Security: run orals in person where security matters and use several question versions, because remote orals may be open to real-time AI help and avatars [S001], [S104], [R95].
evidence_status_basis: Short structured orals were implemented in computing courses (computing = Y in tested_redesigns.md): 10-minute individual vivas with live modification requests for over 750 students [R80]; a structured viva within the TAP redesign for 60 students, with descriptive score and integrity-score changes [R81]; and TA-run live checkoffs with scripted questions and rubrics for 237 students, with duration and survey data [R95]. An automated, submission-specific viva was evaluated against human grading with over 250 students, but not for integrity [S156]. A take-home exam with a follow-up viva was evaluated outside computing [S117]. The sampled-viva element rests on a single computing exam study that is not in the tested-redesign index and did not measure its effect on cheating [S009], so sampling as such remains a proposal.
risks_and_limits: An oral checks understanding at one moment; it does not show who produced each part of the work or how AI was used unless logs or repositories are examined [R79], [R81]. No study tested covert AI use during a live or remote oral. Sampling lowers cost but means most students are not checked, and its deterrent effect is unmeasured [S009]. Viva scores may partly reflect anxiety or language, and all computing evidence is single-cohort and descriptive without control groups [R81], [R80], [R95].
